review_notes: I read the whole file and the simp attributes in ScalarExtension.lean (map_of, map_ofClass, map_of_self for both ProjectiveClass and K0). I grepped the repo for uses of the flagged lemmas. All uses I found are explicit `rw`/`simp only` calls (Product.lean lines 404, 560, 594, 793, and the K0ProductEquivalenceClient tests). So removing @[simp] from them should not break those callers, although I did not check other downstream files. I did not run Lean. The claims about simp behaviour come from reading the rewrite rules, not from observed simp traces. The other @[simp] lemmas (the *_apply ones) look fine. Lemmas such as piEquiv_symm_ofClass are not simp, which is reasonable.

findings.excerpt: ofClass (Ri i) (ProjectiveClass.piEquiv Ri a i) := by
findings.problem: This @[simp] lemma has a right-hand side that is not in simp normal form. Its RHS contains `ProjectiveClass.piEquiv Ri a i`, which the simp lemma `ProjectiveClass.piEquiv_apply` rewrites to `ProjectiveClass.map (Pi.evalRingHom Ri i) a`. Its LHS is also rewritten first by `K0.piEquiv_apply` and then by the simp lemma `K0.map_ofClass`, giving `ofClass (Ri i) (ProjectiveClass.map (Pi.evalRingHom Ri i) a)`. The lemma's own proof shows it follows from those three existing simp lemmas. So it competes with them and, as a simp lemma, adds nothing. If it fires first, it puts an unfolded `ProjectiveClass.piEquiv … a i` into the goal, and simp must then rewrite that back.
findings.proposed_change: Remove @[simp] from `K0.piEquiv_ofClass` and keep it as a plain lemma for `rw`. The simp normal form is already `ofClass (Ri i) (ProjectiveClass.map (Pi.evalRingHom Ri i) a)`, reached via `piEquiv_apply` and `map_ofClass`. Alternatively, state the lemma with `ProjectiveClass.map (Pi.evalRingHom Ri i) a` on the RHS if a simp-normal statement is wanted.
findings.benefit: There is one canonical rewrite path for `K0.piEquiv` applied to a class generator. The simp set no longer has an overlapping lemma whose RHS needs further rewriting, and simp traces are easier to predict.

findings.excerpt:
(ofClass R (ProjectiveClass.prodEquiv R S a).1,
        ofClass S (ProjectiveClass.prodEquiv R S a).2) := by
findings.problem: This @[simp] lemma has a non-normal RHS. The projections `(ProjectiveClass.prodEquiv R S a).1` and `.2` are rewritten by the simp lemma `ProjectiveClass.prodEquiv_apply` to `map (RingHom.fst R S) a` and `map (RingHom.snd R S) a`. Its LHS is rewritten by `K0.prodEquiv_apply` and `K0.map_ofClass` to `(ofClass R (ProjectiveClass.map fst a), ofClass S (ProjectiveClass.map snd a))`. The proof is exactly `simp only [prodEquiv_apply, ProjectiveClass.prodEquiv_apply, map_ofClass]`, so the lemma is subsumed by the existing simp set. It does not describe the form that simp actually produces.
findings.proposed_change: Remove @[simp] from `K0.prodEquiv_ofClass` and keep it for explicit `rw`, which the tests and `prodEquiv_symm_ofClass` use. Or restate its RHS as `(ofClass R (ProjectiveClass.map (RingHom.fst R S) a), ofClass S (ProjectiveClass.map (RingHom.snd R S) a))`.
findings.benefit: Simp has a single canonical normal form for the K₀ decomposition of a class generator, and no lemma re-introduces `ProjectiveClass.prodEquiv` projections that simp must then unfold.

findings.excerpt: simpa only [piEquiv_apply] using map_of (Pi.evalRingHom Ri i) M
findings.problem: Four `*_of_module` lemmas are tagged @[simp]: `ProjectiveClass.piEquiv_of_module`, `ProjectiveClass.prodEquiv_of_module`, `K0.piEquiv_of_module` and `K0.prodEquiv_of_module`. Each is a direct consequence of the simp lemmas `piEquiv_apply` or `prodEquiv_apply` (same namespace) followed by `map_of` (also simp). The proofs are just `simpa only [piEquiv_apply] using map_of …` or `simp only [prodEquiv_apply, map_of]`. The LHS `piEquiv Ri (of M) i` also matches the more general `piEquiv_apply`, so two simp lemmas compete for the same redex. Which one fires first is not specified, and they give the same result only because `map_of` finishes the job. This is redundant simp surface.
findings.proposed_change: Remove @[simp] from the four `*_of_module` lemmas and leave `piEquiv_apply`/`prodEquiv_apply` plus `map_of` as the simp route. Keep the lemmas as plain named statements, since the tests and `prodEquiv_symm_of_module` use them via `rw`.
findings.benefit: There is one simp path for each decomposition applied to a module generator. Removing the redundant lemmas leaves a smaller simp set that does not depend on lemma ordering.
